questions.question: What are real-world examples of the Observer pattern in Java?
questions.title: Observer Pattern Real-World Examples in Java
questions.direct_answer: Observer-style APIs in Java include Swing and JavaFX listeners, JavaBeans `PropertyChangeListener`, servlet lifecycle listeners, and Spring application events. In Spring, `ApplicationEventPublisher` hands an event to the configured multicaster and matching `@EventListener` methods receive it. Delivery is synchronous by default but can be configured differently. `@TransactionalEventListener` binds delivery to a transaction phase; its default is `AFTER_COMMIT` when a transaction exists.

sections.title: Observer Pattern in the Java Ecosystem
sections.content:
Java uses observer-style relationships in many listener APIs. A UI component keeps or delegates to registered action listeners; `PropertyChangeSupport` notifies property listeners; servlet containers call registered lifecycle listeners.

Spring application events provide a container-managed form. A publisher submits an event, the application event multicaster finds listeners by event type, and `@EventListener` methods handle it. The default multicaster calls listeners in the publishing thread, but applications can configure an executor or use supported asynchronous handling.

`@TransactionalEventListener` is different from a normal listener: it is tied to a transaction phase and defaults to `AFTER_COMMIT`. Without an active transaction it normally does not run unless fallback execution is enabled. After-commit callbacks are not a substitute for an outbox when an external message must be delivered reliably.

sections.title: Spring Event System as Observer Pattern
Observer Implementations You'll Meet in Java
sections.content:
amber|Swing / JavaFX|~UI events|addActionListener|button is subject|listener is observer
blue|Spring events|~Business events|ApplicationEventPublisher|@EventListener methods|@TransactionalEventListener for commit
emerald|JavaBeans|~Property changes|PropertyChangeListener|data binding|PropertyChangeSupport helper
violet|Deprecated|~Avoid this one|java.util.Observable|removed in Java 9|was a class, not an interface

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `java.util.Observable`.** It's deprecated since Java 9. Use Spring events or `PropertyChangeSupport`.
- **Assuming `@EventListener` is async.** It runs synchronously in the publisher's thread; add `@Async` (with `@EnableAsync`) for background execution.
- **Ignoring transaction boundaries.** A plain `@EventListener` can run before the DB commit. If the transaction rolls back, you've already emailed the customer. Use `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)`.
- **Only quoting stock-ticker textbook examples.** Name real APIs — that's what separates a fresher who has used Spring from one who memorized a diagram.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Java listener APIs are common Observer-style examples
- Spring events route by event type through an application event multicaster
- Spring delivery is synchronous by default but is configurable
- `@TransactionalEventListener` binds a listener to a transaction phase and defaults to `AFTER_COMMIT`
- Use a transactional outbox or equivalent when database state and external delivery must be reliable together

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Common Observer-style examples are UI action listeners, `PropertyChangeListener`, servlet lifecycle listeners, and Spring application events. In Spring, `ApplicationEventPublisher` hands an event to the configured multicaster, which finds matching `@EventListener` methods. For example, an `OrderPlaced` event can update an in-process read model in the publishing thread. The default delivery is synchronous, although an executor or asynchronous listener can change that behavior. `@TransactionalEventListener` ties a callback to a transaction phase and defaults to after commit when a transaction exists; without a transaction it normally does not run unless fallback execution is enabled. For reliable publication to Kafka or another external system, an after-commit callback alone does not solve the dual-write problem, so I would consider an outbox.

questions.question: What are the potential problems with the Observer pattern?
questions.title: Observer pattern problems
questions.direct_answer: Observer can create hidden control flow, expensive or cascading notifications, implementation-dependent ordering, failure coupling, concurrency problems, and listener lifecycle leaks. A strong reference leaks only when the subject outlives a listener that should have been removed. Define delivery timing and error policy, keep payloads stable, manage registration, and use a suitable snapshot or synchronization strategy.

sections.title: Observer Pattern Trade-offs and Problems
sections.content:
Observer reduces direct knowledge of concrete listeners, but the reaction path becomes less visible. One state change may trigger several callbacks, and a slow, failing, or re-entrant observer can affect the publisher when delivery is synchronous.

Ordering depends on the implementation; code should not rely on it unless the contract defines it. Concurrent registration and notification need a snapshot or synchronization policy, while mutable payloads can let one observer affect another.

A listener leak occurs when a long-lived subject retains a strong reference to an observer whose useful lifetime ended. Explicit registration handles, cleanup, weak-listener designs, or container-managed lifecycle can address it. An observer does not leak merely because it is registered; the mismatch in lifetimes is the problem.

sections.title: The lapsed listener leak — register, never remove
Fix — provide detach, or use weak references
Observer's Five Failure Modes
sections.content:
amber|Lapsed listener|~Memory leak|subject keeps strong refs|observer never detaches|fix: removeObserver / WeakReference
blue|Order undefined|~Fragile dependencies|no run-order guarantee|observers coupled implicitly|fix: make observers independent
emerald|Performance|~O(n) per change|slow observers block subject|hot update paths suffer|fix: async / batching
rose|Cascade & threads|~Hard to debug|A->B->C update chains|ConcurrentModificationException|fix: copy-on-write, no loops

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Never calling `removeObserver`.** Registering in a constructor and assuming GC will clean up — it won't, because the subject still references the observer.
- **Hidden ordering dependencies.** Writing observer A to assume B already ran. Notification order isn't guaranteed, so this is a flaky bug.
- **Slow synchronous observers.** Doing a network/DB call inside `update()` blocks the subject and every later observer. Offload to `@Async` or an executor.
- **Plain `ArrayList` under concurrency.** Iterating during a concurrent `add` throws `ConcurrentModificationException`; use `CopyOnWriteArrayList`.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Notifications can hide control flow and create cascades
- Slow or failing synchronous observers can delay or fail the publisher
- Ordering is implementation-specific unless the contract defines it
- Concurrent registration, state, and payload mutation need explicit rules
- Strong listener references leak when the subject outlives observers that should be removed

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Observer trades direct coupling for indirect control flow. For example, one `OrderUpdated` callback may synchronously trigger inventory, email, and analytics handlers, so one slow or failing handler can delay the original operation. Recursive updates and ordering assumptions can also make the path hard to follow. If registration and notification happen concurrently, the observer list and subject state need a clear snapshot or locking design, and mutable payloads can let listeners interfere. The lifecycle problem occurs when a long-lived subject holds a strong reference to an observer that should have been removed; that mismatch prevents collection. I define timing, ordering, failure, retry, and cleanup policy rather than assuming the pattern provides them.

questions.question: How does the Observer pattern differ from the Pub/Sub messaging pattern?
questions.title: Observer vs Pub/Sub
questions.direct_answer: Observer usually describes an object that maintains a subscription relationship and notifies listeners through a known contract. Publish/subscribe describes communication through a topic or event channel so publishers address the channel rather than subscriber objects. A broker, separate processes, and asynchronous delivery are common Pub/Sub choices, not universal requirements; an in-process synchronous event bus can also be publish/subscribe.

sections.title: Observer vs Pub/Sub Architecture
sections.content:
Observer and publish/subscribe both distribute notifications, but they emphasize different coupling.

In a classic Observer design, a subject owns or uses the subscription mechanism and invokes an observer contract. Subject and observers are normally in the same process, although the abstract pattern does not require one transport.

In publish/subscribe, producers publish to an event type, topic, or channel rather than addressing subscribers. An intermediary routes events. Kafka and RabbitMQ add durable, cross-process, asynchronous messaging, but an in-process event bus can also implement Pub/Sub, and a broker is not the definition by itself.

Choose from delivery guarantees, ordering, failure isolation, process boundaries, and lifecycle—not only from the pattern label.

sections.title: Observer vs Pub/Sub
sections.content:
| Aspect | Classic Observer | Publish/Subscribe |
|---|---|---|
| Addressing | Subject invokes an observer contract | Publisher sends to a topic, event type, or channel |
| Subscription | Often owned by the subject | Often owned by an intermediary/event bus |
| Process boundary | Commonly in-process | Can be in-process or cross-process |
| Timing | Often synchronous | Can be synchronous or asynchronous |
| Broker | Not typical | Optional in-process bus or external broker |
| Guarantees | Defined by implementation | Defined by bus/broker and consumer design |

sections.title: Which One Do You Need?
sections.content:
amber|Observer|~Same JVM|direct references|synchronous default|Spring ApplicationEvent
blue|Pub/Sub|~Across services|broker in the middle|asynchronous + durable|Kafka, RabbitMQ
emerald|The litmus test|~Is there a broker?|no broker -> Observer|broker -> Pub/Sub|name the tech aloud
violet|Scaling|~Why it matters|Observer: one process|Pub/Sub: scale consumers|add subscribers freely

sections.title: Observer — in-process Spring event
Pub/Sub — broker decouples separate services
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling Spring events Pub/Sub.** `ApplicationEvent` has no broker and is single-JVM — it's Observer. True Pub/Sub needs Kafka/RabbitMQ.
- **Using a broker for same-process events.** Adding Kafka to talk between two beans in one app buys network latency and ops burden for nothing.
- **Expecting Pub/Sub to be synchronous.** After `send()`, consumers may process seconds later. Don't assume the work is done when the publish returns.
- **Forgetting durability differences.** Observer notifications vanish if the process dies; broker messages can persist and be replayed.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Observer usually connects a subject to subscribed listener objects
- Pub/Sub addresses a topic, channel, or event type rather than a subscriber
- Brokers and asynchronous cross-process delivery are common, not defining requirements
- An in-process event bus may still be publish/subscribe
- Compare ordering, durability, retries, back pressure, and lifecycle for the actual system

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Classic Observer usually has a subject maintain or use subscriptions and invoke an observer interface when state changes. Publish/subscribe makes the publisher address a topic, channel, or event type instead of subscriber objects, and an intermediary routes the event. For example, a Swing button calls its registered action listeners directly, while an order service may publish to a Kafka topic whose consumers run in other processes. Kafka or RabbitMQ are familiar Pub/Sub systems, but a broker and separate processes are not required by the term; an in-process event bus can also be Pub/Sub. I compare timing, durability, ordering, retries, failure isolation, and lifecycle rather than saying Observer is always synchronous and Pub/Sub is always remote.

questions.question: How would you make an Observer implementation thread-safe in Java?
questions.title: Thread-safe Observer in Java
questions.direct_answer: There is no single thread-safe Observer implementation. Protect both the observer collection and the subject state according to their access pattern. `CopyOnWriteArrayList` gives snapshot iteration and is useful when notifications greatly outnumber registrations; a locked snapshot or immutable subscription registry may be better when writes are frequent. Do not hold internal locks while calling unknown observer code, and define ordering, re-entrancy, exception, and visibility rules.

sections.title: Thread Safety in Observer Pattern
sections.content:
Thread safety covers more than avoiding `ConcurrentModificationException`. A subject must decide which state snapshot a notification represents, how concurrent register/remove operations affect that cycle, and whether observers may re-enter the subject.

`CopyOnWriteArrayList` makes iteration over a stable snapshot simple and suits a small list with many notifications and rare registration changes. Each write copies the backing array, so it can be expensive for frequent changes or large lists. Another design copies a normal list while holding a lock, releases the lock, and then calls the snapshot.

Never hold the subject's internal lock while invoking unknown observer code; a callback may block, throw, or call back into the subject. Define how one listener failure affects the rest and whether notification order is meaningful. `AtomicReference` helps only for a state that can be replaced atomically; several related fields may need an immutable snapshot or lock.

sections.title: Not thread-safe — plain ArrayList under concurrency
Thread-safe — CopyOnWriteArrayList + AtomicReference
Thread-Safe Observer Choices
sections.content:
amber|CopyOnWriteArrayList|~The observer list|lock-free reads|writes copy the array|great: rare writes, frequent reads
blue|AtomicReference|~Single-field state|getAndSet is atomic|no synchronized needed|use for one value
emerald|synchronized getters|~Multi-field state|consistent snapshots|only when fields relate|keep critical section small
rose|No lock on callback|~Avoid deadlock|release lock first|then call observers|observer may call back

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Synchronizing everything**, including the notify loop — frequent notifications then serialize and throughput collapses.
- **Sticking with `ArrayList`** and assuming rare registration means no concurrency issue — a scheduled job plus an HTTP request will hit the exception.
- **Parallelizing notification carelessly** with `parallelStream()` when observers share state — you trade one race for another.
- **Holding a lock during observer callbacks** — if an observer calls back into the subject, you can deadlock.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Protect the observer registry and the subject state as separate concerns
- `CopyOnWriteArrayList` suits many reads or notifications and rare writes
- A locked snapshot can suit other access patterns
- Release internal locks before invoking observer callbacks
- Define visibility, ordering, re-entrancy, and failure policy

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A thread-safe Observer design needs an explicit concurrency contract: which state snapshot is sent, what a concurrent add or remove means, and how one listener failure affects the rest. For example, `CopyOnWriteArrayList` works well for a small configuration-listener registry that is notified often but changed rarely, because iteration sees a stable snapshot; it is not a universal answer because every write copies the array. Another option is to copy a guarded list under a lock and invoke the snapshot after releasing that lock. Unknown listener code should not run while the subject's internal lock is held because it may block, throw, or re-enter. Subject state may use an atomic immutable snapshot or a lock depending on how many fields must stay consistent.

questions.question: What is the Observer pattern and when should you use it?
questions.title: Observer Pattern Explained
questions.direct_answer: The **Observer pattern** sets up a one-to-many dependency: when a **subject** changes state, it automatically notifies all registered **observers** through an interface — so neither side hardcodes the other. Use it when several components must react to a change without the subject knowing their concrete types, like an order update fanning out to email, inventory, and analytics.

sections.title: Observer Pattern Fundamentals
sections.content:
The **Observer pattern** creates a one-to-many relationship: a **subject** (the watched thing) notifies many **observers** (the watchers) whenever its state changes.

It's like subscribing to a channel — when the creator posts, every subscriber is notified, and the creator never maintains a hand-coded list of who to call. The pattern leans on **interfaces**: the subject only knows observers implement an `Observer` contract, not their concrete classes. That **loose coupling** lets you add or remove observers at runtime without touching the subject.

The payoff is **separation of concerns** — the subject does its core job while observers react independently. In a cart service, placing an order (state change) can notify inventory, email, and analytics observers without the order code ever referencing them.

sections.title: Without Observer — subject hardcodes every dependency
With Observer — subject knows only the interface
Observer Pattern at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Subject|~The watched thing|holds observer list|attach / detach / notify|knows only the interface
blue|Observer|~The watcher|implements update|reacts independently|many can register
emerald|Loose coupling|~The whole point|subject -> interface only|add types freely|no recompile of subject
violet|Lifecycle|~Avoid leaks|always provide detach|unregister when done|or use Spring's container

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting to unregister observers** — the lapsed listener leak; always provide and call `removeObserver`.
- **Modifying the observer list during notification** — removing inside `update()` on a plain `ArrayList` throws `ConcurrentModificationException`; iterate a copy or use `CopyOnWriteArrayList`.
- **Observers depending on each other** — relying on order breaks the independence the pattern promises.
- **Calling the concrete services directly** — if `Cart` imports `EmailService`, it isn't Observer, it's tight coupling.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Subject** manages observers (attach/detach/notify) without knowing their types.
- **Observer interface** declares `update`, enabling polymorphic notification.
- **Loose coupling** — add observer types with zero subject changes.
- **Dynamic subscription** — register/unregister at runtime.
- **Push vs pull** — send data with the notification, or send a signal and let observers query.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The Observer pattern lets one object notify many others when something changes, without hardcoding who those others are. It's a subscription model — observers register their interest and get updates automatically. The key benefit is loose coupling: the subject only knows that observers implement a common interface, not their concrete classes. Let me use a cart service example. When a user adds an item to their cart, you might need to reserve inventory, recalculate shipping, and log analytics. Without Observer, the Cart class would directly call inventoryService dot reserve, shippingCalculator dot update, and analyticsLogger dot log — that's tight coupling, and adding a new reaction means editing Cart. With Observer, Cart just loops over its registered observers and calls their update method. Each service implements the observer interface and reacts on its own. You can add a recommendation service later without touching Cart at all. In Spring Boot you'd express this with ApplicationEventPublisher — you publish a CartUpdatedEvent and mark listener methods with at EventListener, and Spring registers them for you. The biggest pitfall to mention is the memory leak. If observers never unregister, they can't be garbage collected even when you're done with them, because the subject's list still holds them. So always provide a removeObserver method and call it when the observer's life ends. And if you're iterating the observer list during notification, use a copy or CopyOnWriteArrayList so you don't hit a ConcurrentModificationException when an observer removes itself.

questions.question: What is the difference between the push and pull models in Observer pattern?
questions.title: Observer Pattern: Push vs Pull Model
questions.direct_answer: In push delivery, the notification contains data chosen by the subject. In pull delivery, the notification is small and the observer queries the subject or another source. Push can give a stable event snapshot but may include unused fields; pull can reduce payload size but increases coupling, extra reads, and the risk that state changes before it is read. Many systems use a deliberate hybrid.

sections.title: Push vs Pull Notification Strategies
sections.content:
The **push model** places relevant state in the notification. Each observer sees the event snapshot chosen by the subject, which is useful when the value at the time of change matters. A large or unstable payload can couple consumers to fields they do not need.

The **pull model** sends a small signal or reference and lets an observer query for details. It can avoid a large payload, but it adds knowledge of the query source, may perform repeated work, and can observe newer state rather than the state that caused the notification.

A hybrid is common: push an identifier, version, and essential changed values, then let consumers fetch other details when needed. The contract should say whether the event represents immutable historical data or only a signal.

sections.title: Push Model vs Pull Model
sections.content:
| Aspect | Push | Pull |
|---|---|---|
| Data transfer | Subject sends all relevant data | Subject sends a minimal signal |
| Observer role | Receives data passively | Queries the subject for data |
| Efficiency | May ship unused data | Fetches only what's needed |
| Implementation | Simpler — data in the call | Observer must hold subject reference |
| Best for | Small change, all need it | Large state, observers need subsets |

sections.title: Push vs Pull at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Push|~Data in the call|update(fullObject)|simplest to write|may ship unused data
blue|Pull|~Signal + reference|update(subject)|observer fetches slice|needs subject reference
emerald|Choose push|~When|change is small|all observers need it|Spring events do this
violet|Choose pull|~When|state is large|observers need subsets|avoids wasted transfer

sections.title: Push — data travels in the update call
Pull — signal only, observer fetches what it needs
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Always choosing push** because it's easier — broadcasting a 5KB object to 20 observers that need one field wastes memory and CPU.
- **Pull without a subject reference** — if `update()` carries no reference, observers have nothing to query.
- **Mixing push and pull inconsistently** — passing some data and expecting observers to fetch the rest muddies the contract; pick one.
- **Pushing mutable state** — handing observers your live collection lets them mutate the subject; return copies.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Push carries state in the notification
- Pull sends a signal and observers query another source
- Push preserves a chosen snapshot but can over-couple payloads
- Pull can add reads, coupling, and race-with-later-state problems
- A hybrid can push identity or version and let consumers fetch optional details

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Push and pull describe where observers get the data. In push, the notification contains values selected by the subject, so every listener can see the same event snapshot. For example, `PriceChanged(productId, oldPrice, newPrice, version)` preserves the values that caused the event. In pull, the notification is small and each listener queries the subject or another source; that may reduce payload size but adds reads and can return state newer than the triggering change. Many systems use a hybrid by pushing an ID, version, and essential values, then fetching optional details. I choose based on snapshot accuracy, payload stability, query cost, and consumer coupling.

questions.question: How do you implement Observer pattern in Java from scratch?
questions.title: Implementing Observer Pattern in Java
questions.direct_answer: Define an observer callback and a subject or subscription API, store registrations, update state, capture the intended listener and state snapshot, then invoke callbacks according to a documented timing and error policy. Copying a list avoids self-removal problems during one-thread iteration but is not by itself a complete thread-safety design. Provide a registration handle or removal method when observer lifetimes differ.

sections.title: Implementing Observer from Scratch
sections.content:
Four pieces: the **`Observer` interface** (how the subject calls observers), the **`Subject` interface** (attach/detach/notify), a **concrete subject** holding the observer list, and **concrete observers** with reaction logic.

Two details freshers miss. First, **timing**: change the subject's state *before* calling `notifyObservers`, so observers see the new value. Second, **safe iteration**: if an observer detaches itself inside `update()`, iterating the live `ArrayList` throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. Iterate a copy (`List.copyOf`) or use `CopyOnWriteArrayList`. And always provide `detach` so observers can unregister and be garbage-collected.

sections.title: Build It Step by Step
sections.content:
| Step | What to do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Define `Observer { update(...) }` | the notification contract |
| 2 | Define `Subject { attach, detach, notifyObservers }` | manage subscriptions |
| 3 | Concrete subject holds a `List<Observer>` | track who to notify |
| 4 | On change: update state, then notify | observers see fresh data |
| 5 | Iterate a copy / `CopyOnWriteArrayList` | avoid `ConcurrentModificationException` |
| 6 | Implement concrete observers | the actual reactions |

sections.title: Complete Observer Implementation
The Four Moving Parts
sections.content:
amber|Observer interface|~The contract|one method: update|push or pull data|implemented by reactions
blue|Subject interface|~Manages observers|attach / detach|notifyObservers|standard surface
emerald|Concrete subject|~Owns the state|holds List<Observer>|notify AFTER change|copy before iterating
violet|Concrete observers|~The reactions|email, SMS, log|independent of each other|detach when done

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Iterating the live list.** An observer detaching itself in `update()` throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. Use `List.copyOf(observers)` or `CopyOnWriteArrayList`.
- **No `detach` method.** Without unregister, observers leak (the lapsed listener problem).
- **Notifying before the state change.** Observers then read stale data; always update state first.
- **Coupling observers to each other.** Don't assume one observer ran before another — order isn't guaranteed.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Define the callback payload and subscription lifecycle
- Update state and capture the intended immutable snapshot before notification
- Iterate a snapshot if callbacks may add or remove listeners
- Copying alone does not make concurrent state and registration thread-safe
- Define callback order, exception behavior, re-entrancy, and cleanup

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I define an observer callback, a way to register and remove observers, and a subject that owns the registrations. When state changes, the subject first creates the event or immutable state snapshot, then captures the listeners for that notification cycle and invokes them according to a documented policy. For example, iterating `List.copyOf(listeners)` lets one callback remove itself without changing the current iteration, but that copy alone does not make concurrent registration and subject state safe; those still need a lock or concurrent structure. I provide a removal handle when listener lifetimes differ, avoid holding internal locks during callbacks, and decide what ordering and one listener exception mean.

questions.question: How does the Observer pattern relate to Java's EventListener and Spring's event system?
questions.title: Observer Pattern vs EventListener vs Spring Events
questions.direct_answer: Java listener APIs and Spring application events are Observer-style mechanisms: producers publish or signal an event and registered handlers react through a common contract. Spring uses an application event multicaster and dependency injection rather than a subject directly storing each concrete listener. Delivery is synchronous by default but configurable; transaction-bound and asynchronous listeners have different failure and consistency rules.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Java listener interfaces are direct Observer-style contracts
- Spring routes application events through a container-managed multicaster
- Default Spring delivery is synchronous in the publisher's thread
- Async delivery changes error propagation, context, ordering, and completion timing
- Transaction-bound listeners default to `AFTER_COMMIT`; reliable external delivery may need an outbox

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Java event listeners and Spring application events are Observer-style mechanisms, but Spring inserts a container-managed event multicaster. A publisher hands over an event, and matching `@EventListener` methods are registered by the container, so the publisher has no concrete listener references. For example, a normal `OrderPlaced` listener runs in the publishing thread with the default multicaster, so its exception can affect the publish call. Configured asynchronous handling changes ordering, context, and error propagation. `@TransactionalEventListener` binds delivery to a transaction phase and defaults to after commit when a transaction exists. That callback is useful for transaction-aware work, but it does not by itself make an external publish atomic with the database, so reliable integration may need an outbox.

sections.title: Understand the decision
sections.content:
Java's listener interfaces are a direct Observer-style API: a source accepts listeners and invokes their callback when an event occurs.

Spring application events add an intermediary managed by the container. `ApplicationEventPublisher` hands an event to the application event multicaster, and methods registered with `@EventListener` are selected by type. The publisher does not need references to concrete listeners. With the default multicaster, listeners run in the publishing thread; executor-backed or `@Async` handling changes timing and exception behavior.

`@TransactionalEventListener` binds a listener to a transaction phase and defaults to `AFTER_COMMIT`. It normally requires an active transaction unless fallback execution is enabled. An after-commit callback still does not make a database change and an external message atomic; use an outbox or another reliability pattern when that guarantee matters.

sections.title: Spring Events Mapped to Observer Roles
Observer Roles in Spring
sections.content:
amber|Subject|~Publishes|ApplicationEventPublisher|inject + publishEvent|knows only the event type
blue|Observer|~Reacts|@EventListener method|auto-registered on scan|no manual attach
emerald|Notification data|~The payload|event record/POJO|replaces update params|immutable is best
violet|Spring extras|~Beyond classic|@Async for background|@TransactionalEventListener|AFTER_COMMIT safety

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming `@EventListener` is async.** It's synchronous by default; add `@Async` (with `@EnableAsync`) for background work.
- **Publishing then reading uncommitted data.** A plain listener may run before commit. Use `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)`.
- **Ignoring exception propagation.** In synchronous mode, a listener throwing can stop later listeners; handle errors per listener.
- **Thinking Spring events are Pub/Sub.** No broker, single JVM — it's Observer.

sections.title: How the choices differ
sections.content: **Observer** is in-process: the subject holds direct references to observers in the same JVM and calls them, usually synchronously. **Pub/Sub** puts a **message broker** (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SNS) between publishers and subscribers, so they're fully decoupled, run in different processes, and communicate asynchronously. Spring's `ApplicationEvent` is Observer, not true Pub/Sub.
